Female Japanese silver-biddy attain a larger ultimate body size than males, with the maximum recorded standard length for females reaching 21.3 centimeters [Li = 21.3 centimeters]. In contrast, males typically achieve a slightly smaller asymptotic length, with the largest documented individuals measuring 20.6 centimeters [Li = 20.6 centimeters] in standard length. This pattern of female-biased sexual size dimorphism is widespread among gerreid fishes and is often interpreted as a consequence of fecundity selection, where larger body cavities accommodate greater ovarian volume. The growth trajectories that culminate in these terminal sizes reflect a protracted juvenile period during which individuals allocate resources primarily to somatic expansion. Field surveys conducted across the species’ range in coastal East Asia indicate that these maxima are rarely surpassed, suggesting a strong upper bound imposed by local environmental conditions or energetic limitations. The reported values align closely with those documented for the congener Gerres oyena, though intraspecific variation is notable across latitudinal gradients, with populations in warmer, more productive waters tending toward the upper end of the range.

At the onset of reproductive competence, individuals of Gerres equulus display a standard length of approximately 14.1 centimeters [Lp = approximately 14.1 centimeters], a milestone that marks the transition to the mature portion of the population. This length at puberty is appreciably higher than the size at which many other coastal spariform species first develop functional gonads, suggesting a relatively conservative maturation schedule. The corresponding body mass at this developmental stage has been estimated at 76.2 grams [Wwp = 76.2 grams], a figure derived from length-weight regressions fitted to local catch data. These regressions reveal a near-isometric scaling relationship, and the predicted mass at the pubertal length is consistent with the observed condition of early-stage gravid individuals in trawl samples from the South China Sea. Reaching this threshold likely requires several growing seasons, and the energetic investment necessary to cross this size boundary may delay the onset of the first spawning event relative to faster-growing species that share similar inshore habitats. Variation in local food availability may modulate the age at which this critical size is attained, with individuals in richer environments reaching it earlier.

Reproduction in Japanese silver-biddy begins with the release of small, pelagic eggs, each fertilised externally following broadcast spawning events. The wet weight of a newly hatched yolk-sac larva, calculated from an assumed oocyte diameter of 0.8 millimeters, is approximately 0.00027 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00027 grams]. This minute starting mass places the species among the smaller propagule producers within the Gerreidae, and the resultant lecithotrophic larvae must rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first days post-eclosion. The period following chorion rupture is therefore critical, as the non-feeding larva must complete mouth opening and retinal differentiation before its yolk supply is exhausted. The hatchling mass is low enough that starvation mortality during the transition to exogenous feeding may be a significant bottleneck, particularly in oligotrophic waters where suitable planktonic prey items are scarce. Field collections of ichthyoplankton across the Western Pacific have occasionally recovered prolarvae at sizes consistent with this mass estimate, confirming that the value falls within the empirically observed range for wild-spawned cohorts.

As the fish approach their terminal size, the corresponding ultimate wet weight for females has been estimated at 271.5 grams [Wwi = 271.5 grams], a value that integrates the length-weight relationship characteristic of the species. This asymptotic body mass represents the maximum somatic investment an individual can achieve under typical field conditions, and it is substantially greater than the mass at puberty, reflecting the considerable post-maturational growth that Gerres equulus continues to undergo. In males, the equivalent maximum mass is somewhat lower, consistent with the sexual dimorphism observed in standard length. This incremental increase in body mass after the onset of reproductive activity is a common life-history pattern among iteroparous teleosts, allowing individuals to progressively enhance their reproductive output with age. Tag-recapture studies indicate that individuals approach this asymptotic mass gradually, with growth rates decelerating markedly as the fish near their maximum size. The fat reserves accumulated by these larger individuals likely buffer against seasonal food shortages and support the energetic demands of repeated spawning events across multiple breeding seasons.

Longevity in Gerres equulus has been estimated from otolith-based age determinations conducted at a mean annual water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], yielding a maximum lifespan of approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years]. This longevity is moderate compared to some gerreid congeners from cooler, higher-latitude environments, where slower metabolic rates are associated with extended lifespans. At the 18 °C thermal regime typical of the species’ subtropical range, age-structured population models suggest that natural mortality accumulates gradually, with senescence becoming evident only after the eighth year. The oldest individuals recovered in fishery-independent surveys have consistently fallen within this decadal window, and no verified specimen has exceeded this threshold. The trade-off between this lifespan and the species’ relatively high fecundity is consistent with a broader pattern observed among iteroparous coastal fishes, where extended reproductive windows compensate for modest per-event fecundity. This decadal life expectancy shapes the population’s response to fishing pressure, as removals of older, larger individuals disproportionately affect the reproductive potential of the stock.
